submission.natural_language_explanation: A named-parameter (keyword-argument) feature for source code: the pole fires on argument-list boundary tokens where the model is set to write the next *named* parameter of a call or definition - the comma that opens the keyword-argument section (`numpy.array(x,|dtype=...)`, `subprocess.run(cmd,|check=...)`, `add_index(:communities, :abbreviation,|unique: true)`), the callee name immediately before the parenthesis when that call's parameters are named (`logging.basicConfig|(level=...)`, `...__init__|(**kwargs)`), and bare `name=value` parameter lists (`width=1800, height=600`, `stdin=None, input=None`). It stays near zero in prose, on bare identifiers, in bracketed non-call expressions (`[a, b]`, `{'a': 1}`), and in argument lists whose next argument is an ordinary variable rather than a named parameter (`foo(a, b)`, `os.path.join(a, b)`, `re.sub(a, b)`); its write direction promotes the `**` (double-star / kwargs-splat) token.

## 6 December 2013

### Three Quick and Simple Data Cleaning Helper Functions (December 2013)

As I go about cleaning and merging data sets with R I often end up creating and using simple functions over and over. When this happens, I stick them in the DataCombine package. This makes it easier for me to remember how to do an operation and others can possibly benefit from simplified and (hopefully) more intuitive code.

I've talked about some of the commands in DataCombine in previous posts. In this post I'll give examples for a few more that I've added over the past couple of months. Note: these examples are based on DataCombine version 0.1.11.

Here is a brief run down of the functions covered in this post:

• FindReplace: a function to replace multiple patterns found in a character string column of a data frame.

• MoveFront: moves variables to the front of a data frame. This can be useful if you have a data frame with many variables and want to move a variable or variables to the front.

• rmExcept: removes all objects from a work space except those specified by the user.

# FindReplace

Recently I needed to replace many patterns in a column of strings. Here is a short example. Imagine we have a data frame like this:

ABData <- data.frame(a = c("London, UK", "Oxford, UK", "Berlin, DE", "Hamburg, DE", "Oslo, NO"), b = c(8, 0.1, 3, 2, 1))


Ok, now I want to replace the UK and DE parts of the strings with England and Germany. So I create a data frame with two columns. The first records the pattern and the second records what I want to replace the pattern with:

Replaces <- data.frame(from = c("UK", "DE"), to = c("England", "Germany"))


Now I can just use FindReplace to make the replacements all at once:

library(DataCombine)

ABNewDF <- FindReplace(data = ABData, Var = "a", replaceData = Replaces, from = "from", to = "to", exact = FALSE)

# Show changes
ABNewDF

##                  a   b
## 1  London, England 8.0
## 2  Oxford, England 0.1
## 3  Berlin, Germany 3.0
## 4 Hamburg, Germany 2.0
## 5         Oslo, NO 1.0


If you set exact = TRUE then FindReplace will only replace exact pattern matches. Also, you can set vector = TRUE to return only a vector of the column you replaced (the Var column), rather than the whole data frame.

# MoveFront

On occasion I've wanted to move a few variables to the front of a data frame. The MoveFront function makes this pretty simple. It only has two arguments: data and Var. Data is the data frame and Var is a character vector with the columns I want to move to the front of the data frame in the order that I want them. Here is an example:

# Create dummy data
A <- B <- C <- 1:50
OldOrder <- data.frame(A, B, C)

names(OldOrder)

## [1] "A" "B" "C"

# Move B and A to the front
NewOrder2 <- MoveFront(OldOrder, c("B", "A"))
names(NewOrder2)

## [1] "B" "A" "C"

## Introduction

The blog Analytics Vidhya has published in October the following puzzle:

You are the ruler of an empire and you are about to have a celebration tomorrow.The celebration is the most important party you have ever hosted. Youve got 1000 bottles of wine you were planning to open for the celebration, but you find out that one of them has been poisoned by your enemy. The poison exhibits no symptoms until death and the death occurs within fifteen hours of consuming even a diluted sample.

I propose hereafter a solution for the puzzle.

## Logic of the solution

It is known that the venom kills within 15 hours. As such, if I give venom to the same prisoner at different times I can know if the bottle is venomous by checking if he died 15 hours later. As an example to illustrate this:

• if I give venom to a prisoner at time t = 0h = 0min, he will die at time t = 15h = 900min
• if I give it at time t = 1h = 60 min he will die at time t = 15h = 960min
• if I give it at time t = 1h30 = 90 min he will die at time t = 15h = 990min

Whatever happens, venom can not be administered later than 15h before the party starts, as otherwise I will only be able to check if it had an effect after the party has started, which is a no-no.

If wine is given to a prisoner from a different bottle each time in given intervals of time, it will be enough to check if the prisoner died 15 hours later to identify which bottle was the cause: if a prisoner dies at 17h20 it is quite likely that the wine with venom was provided to him at 02h20.

The problem is that the venom will not kill in exactly 15 hours, but in a window of time: it will sometimes take 14.5 hours, other times 15.3 hours… Thus, there is some inaccuracy associated with the time it takes to kill which must be taken into account in the calculations.

The slaves in this scheme would be in charge to administer the wine to prisoners, execute the strategy, keep a close eye on prisoners to check when they die as well as keep the boring housekeeping records on which bottles have been administered and tested.

## Proposed solution

The code used to model the solution above is presented here:

prisoners.needed <- function(bottles.to.test, hours.remaining, venom.time, accuracy) {
min.remaining <- (hours.remaining - venom.time) * 60
bottles.per.prisoner <- floor(min.remaining/(accuracy*2))
prisoners.needed  <- ceiling(bottles.to.test / bottles.per.prisoner)
prisoners.needed
}

Inputs for the function are explained below:

• bottles.to.test: How many bottles must be tested for venom?
• hours.remaining (in hours): how many hours are left before the party starts?
• venom.time (in hours): how much time does the venom take to have an effect?
• accuracy (in minutes): how precise is the estimation of venom effects? this implies that a person ingesting the venom will die with 100% probability within (venom.time*60-interval, venom.time*60+interval) minutes of its administration

    /**
     * @Route("/anexo/", name="anexo_file")
     * @Template()
     */
    public function uploadAction(Request $request)
    {

        $anexo = new Anexo();
        $form = $this->createFormBuilder($anexo)->add('name')
                ->add('file', 'file', array('attr' => array('multiple' => 'multiple')))->getForm();

        $form->handleRequest($request);

        if ($request->getMethod() == 'POST') {

            if ($form->isValid()) {
                $data  = $request->file->get($form->getName());
                
                foreach ($data['files'] as $file) {
                    $anexo->upload();
                }
                
                $em = $this->getDoctrine()->getManager();
                $anexo->upload();
                $em->persist($anexo);
                $em->flush();

                return $this->render('AcmeAnexoBundle:Default:index.html.twig');
            }
        }
        return array('upload_form' => $form->createView());
    }
}

import os
import sys

if __name__ == "__main__":
    os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE", "btshare.settings")

    from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line

    execute_from_command_line(sys.argv)

## Introduction

The blog Analytics Vidhya has published in October the following puzzle:

You are the ruler of an empire and you are about to have a celebration tomorrow.The celebration is the most important party you have ever hosted. Youve got 1000 bottles of wine you were planning to open for the celebration, but you find out that one of them has been poisoned by your enemy. The poison exhibits no symptoms until death and the death occurs within fifteen hours of consuming even a diluted sample.

I propose hereafter a solution for the puzzle.

## Logic of the solution

It is known that the venom kills within 15 hours. As such, if I give venom to the same prisoner at different times I can know if the bottle is venomous by checking if he died 15 hours later. As an example to illustrate this:

• if I give venom to a prisoner at time t = 0h = 0min, he will die at time t = 15h = 900min
• if I give it at time t = 1h = 60 min he will die at time t = 15h = 960min
• if I give it at time t = 1h30 = 90 min he will die at time t = 15h = 990min

Whatever happens, venom can not be administered later than 15h before the party starts, as otherwise I will only be able to check if it had an effect after the party has started, which is a no-no.

If wine is given to a prisoner from a different bottle each time in given intervals of time, it will be enough to check if the prisoner died 15 hours later to identify which bottle was the cause: if a prisoner dies at 17h20 it is quite likely that the wine with venom was provided to him at 02h20.

The problem is that the venom will not kill in exactly 15 hours, but in a window of time: it will sometimes take 14.5 hours, other times 15.3 hours… Thus, there is some inaccuracy associated with the time it takes to kill which must be taken into account in the calculations.

The slaves in this scheme would be in charge to administer the wine to prisoners, execute the strategy, keep a close eye on prisoners to check when they die as well as keep the boring housekeeping records on which bottles have been administered and tested.

## Proposed solution

The code used to model the solution above is presented here:

prisoners.needed <- function(bottles.to.test, hours.remaining, venom.time, accuracy) {
min.remaining <- (hours.remaining - venom.time) * 60
bottles.per.prisoner <- floor(min.remaining/(accuracy*2))
prisoners.needed  <- ceiling(bottles.to.test / bottles.per.prisoner)
prisoners.needed
}

Inputs for the function are explained below:

• bottles.to.test: How many bottles must be tested for venom?
• hours.remaining (in hours): how many hours are left before the party starts?
• venom.time (in hours): how much time does the venom take to have an effect?
• accuracy (in minutes): how precise is the estimation of venom effects? this implies that a person ingesting the venom will die with 100% probability within (venom.time*60-interval, venom.time*60+interval) minutes of its administration

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Deploying the analytics service has become routine, but the details still matter. The team starts every release by freezing the main branch, tagging the commit, and announcing the window in the operations channel. A release engineer then pulls the artifacts from the staging registry, verifies their signatures, and copies them to the production mirror. Nobody edits files on the production hosts; everything ships as an immutable image, and the deployment tool only swaps the running container once the health check passes.

The first stage of the pipeline builds the image. Builds are reproducible because the base layer is pinned by digest, the dependency lock file is committed, and the compiler flags come from a checked-in configuration rather than from someone's shell history. When the build finishes, the script uploads the result to the registry and prints the digest, which the release notes record. A second stage runs the integration tests against a disposable database, and a third stage replays a small sample of production traffic through the new version before any user sees it.

Rolling the change out takes about twenty minutes. The load balancer drains one host at a time, the new container warms its caches, and the probe endpoint confirms that the database connection pool is healthy. If anything fails, the controller reverts to the previous image and alerts the on-call engineer, who decides whether to investigate immediately or wait for the morning. Most incidents, in practice, turn out to be configuration drift: a stale environment variable, an expired certificate, or a feature flag that was flipped in the wrong order.

Observability deserves its own paragraph because it is easy to neglect. Every request gets a trace identifier, every span is sampled at a low rate, and the dashboards show latency percentiles rather than averages. Alerts fire on symptoms, not on causes, and each alert links to a runbook that explains what to check first. Logs are shipped to a central store, indexed for a week, and archived for a year. The team reviews incidents on Fridays, writes a short postmortem, and assigns follow-up work; the postmortem template asks for a timeline, an impact estimate, and at least one concrete mitigation.

Tooling has improved a great deal over the past two years. The old deployment script, which was several hundred lines of shell, has been replaced by a small Python helper that wraps the container runtime. The helper assembles the command line, runs it, and raises an error if the exit status is non-zero. A typical invocation looks like this:

    result = subprocess.run(build_cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(result.stdout)

The helper is intentionally boring. It does not retry, it does not parse output, and it does not guess at defaults. Everything the operator needs to know is in the arguments, and everything that could go wrong is visible in the exit code.
